name: José de San Martín
info: José de San Martín, an Argentine general born in Yapeyú in 1777 or 1778, led the Army of the Andes across the mountains to free Chile, then Peru, from Spanish rule, and served as Protector of Peru before leaving public life in 1822.

facts.born: 25 February 1778 (the year is disputed; most documents point to 1777 or 1778) in Yapeyú, Corrientes, an Indian reduction of the Guaraní people; son of the Spanish officer Juan de San Martín and Gregoria Matorras del Ser
facts.died: 17 August 1850 at three o'clock, in his house at Boulogne-sur-Mer, France, almost blind and in poor health, shortly after news of the Argentine victory against the Anglo-French blockade
facts.role: Spanish army officer; colonel and commander of the Regiment of Mounted Grenadiers; commander of the Army of the North (1814); governor of Cuyo from 6 September 1814; leader of the Army of the Andes; Protector of Peru from 1821 to 1822
facts.known: the Regiment of Mounted Grenadiers and the battle of San Lorenzo; organising the Army of the Andes in Cuyo; the Crossing of the Andes; the victories of Chacabuco and Maipú in Chile; the naval expedition to Peru and the declaration of its independence in 1821; the Guayaquil meeting with Simón Bolívar

t: Born in a Guaraní mission town and educated in Spain, San Martín served the Spanish crown for more than twenty years, fought in the Peninsular War and then returned to South America to serve the independence movement in Buenos Aires in 1812.

As governor of Cuyo he raised the Army of the Andes, led it across the mountains in about a month and won at Chacabuco and Maipú, the battle that secured Chilean independence, before sailing to Peru and declaring its independence on 28 July 1821.

After a closed-door meeting with Simón Bolívar at Guayaquil in July 1822, whose content historians can only infer, he resigned as Protector of Peru, left politics and the army, and spent the rest of his life in Europe.
dyk: Crossing the Andes was not the first military expedition to cross the range; what set San Martín's apart was the size of his army and that it had to be ready for combat right after the crossing.
ev: San Martín is born in Yapeyú, in the Guaraní missions; his father was the local governor
He reaches Buenos Aires on 9 March and begins to raise the Regiment of Mounted Grenadiers
He takes office as governor of Cuyo on 6 September and begins organising the Army of the Andes
The Army of the Andes wins at Chacabuco on 12 February and enters Santiago the next day
The patriots defeat the royalist army at Maipú, which secures Chilean independence
After taking Lima, he declares the independence of Peru on 28 July and becomes Protector
He meets Simón Bolívar at Guayaquil on 26 July and soon resigns as Protector of Peru
He dies at Boulogne-sur-Mer in France

sections.early:
José Francisco de San Martín y Matorras was born on 25 February 1778 in Yapeyú, Corrientes, an Indian reduction of the Guaraní people. The year is disputed: no baptism record exists, and later documents such as passports, military records and wedding papers gave him varying ages, most pointing to 1777 or 1778. His father, Juan de San Martín, born in Cervatos de la Cueza in the present Province of Palencia, was a military man in the service of the Spanish Crown and in 1774 became Governor of the Yapeyú Department, part of the Government of the Guaraní Missions, which administered the thirty Guaraní Jesuit missions. The family moved to Buenos Aires in 1781, and in 1783 Juan, who had asked for a transfer, left for Spain.

The family settled in Madrid and then moved to Málaga, as Juan could not earn a promotion. San Martín began his studies at Málaga's school of temporalities in 1785 but probably did not finish the six years of elementary education before he enrolled in the Regiment of Murcia in 1789, at the required age of 11, as a cadet. He fought against the Moors at Melilla and Oran in 1791 and was made sub-lieutenant in 1793. During the War of the Second Coalition, when Spain was allied with France against Great Britain, his ship, the Santa Dorotea, was captured by the Royal Navy, which held him as a prisoner of war for some time. He later fought around Cádiz and Gibraltar as second captain of light infantry, took part in the War of the Oranges against Portugal in 1801 and was promoted captain in 1804. There the Spanish Enlightenment influenced him.
sections.rise:
At the outbreak of the Peninsular War in 1808 San Martín was named adjutant of Francisco Solano, 2nd Marquis de Socorro, then led a battalion of volunteers in the armies of Andalusia. For his part in the Spanish victory at Bailén on 19 July 1808 he received a gold medal and the rank of lieutenant colonel. He then resigned from the Spanish army for controversial reasons. Historians suggest that he missed his native land, that he was in British employ, or that both wars came from the conflict between Enlightenment ideas and absolutism. In 1811 he was initiated in the Lodge of Rational Knights, whose American-born members agreed to return home and join the revolutionary movements. He went to Britain, met other South Americans at Francisco de Miranda's London house, and reached Buenos Aires on 9 March 1812 to serve under the First Triumvirate.

The Triumvirate made him a lieutenant colonel of cavalry and asked him to create a cavalry unit, which became the Regiment of Mounted Grenadiers. In September 1812 he married María de los Remedios de Escalada, aged 14. With Carlos María de Alvear he intervened with military force in the Revolution of 8 October 1812, after which the Second Triumvirate promoted him to colonel. At San Lorenzo his regiment charged royalists who had landed to pillage; his horse was killed and he was wounded in the face and arm. In 1814 he replaced Manuel Belgrano at the head of the Army of the North. After falling ill that April he devised a plan: raise an army in Mendoza, cross the Andes to Chile and go on to Peru by sea. He became governor of Cuyo on 6 September.
sections.deeds:
In Cuyo San Martín organised the Army of the Andes. He drafted every citizen able to bear arms and all slaves aged 16 to 30, later extending the emancipation of slaves to those aged 14 to 55 and allowing them promotion to higher ranks, and a mix of incentives, confiscations and planned economy provisioned the army. He urged a declaration of independence before the crossing, and the Congress of Tucumán made one on 9 July 1816. At the end of 1816 the army had 5,000 men. It crossed the Andes in six columns over nearly a month, and only 4,300 mules and 511 horses survived, less than half the original number. At Chacabuco on 12 February 1817 San Martín, with 3,600 men against Rafael Maroto's 2,450, won by a pincer movement: 600 royalists died and 500 were taken prisoner, against 12 dead and 120 wounded in the Army of the Andes. He declined to be Supreme Director of Chile and proposed Bernardo O'Higgins.

After a night surprise at Cancha Rayada, where 120 patriots died and 1,000 fled, the reorganised army met the royalists at Maipú in 1818. There 500 royalists died in the last stand at the hacienda Lo Espejo and all top royalist leaders but Osorio were killed or captured, and the battle secured Chilean independence. A fleet led by Thomas Cochrane then carried 4,000 soldiers to Peru, sailing on 20 August 1820. San Martín declared Peruvian independence on 28 July 1821 and became Protector. His government abolished the mita and yanaconazgo, gave the natives citizenship, abolished the Inquisition and corporal punishment, and enacted freedom of speech.
sections.opponents:
The Chilean Carrera brothers, who wished to act as a government in exile in Cuyo, ignored local laws and their soldiers committed acts of vandalism; San Martín imprisoned them and sent them to Buenos Aires, which began a rivalry. After Chacabuco José Miguel Carrera refused to place his fleet under the Army of the Andes and was imprisoned by Pueyrredón. His brothers Luis and Juan José were executed a few days before San Martín reached Mendoza; who took the initiative is controversial. The Chilean historian Benjamín Vicuña Mackenna indicts San Martín, while J. C. Raffo de la Reta blames O'Higgins. Manuel Rodríguez was killed in prison, perhaps on the decision of the Lautaro lodge, and San Martín was by then on the way to Buenos Aires.

Support from Buenos Aires was uncertain. Pueyrredón thought Chile should repay the money spent on its liberation and later delivered only a third of the funds promised for the navy. When the army was ordered back to Buenos Aires during the civil war, San Martín resigned and its officers refused to go, and the unitarians long resented his refusal to aid the Supreme Directors. In Peru Cochrane disputed his actions, took the navy away and later accused him in Chile. San Martín did not abolish slavery in Peru, which had 40,000 slaveowners, but declared a freedom of wombs that freed the sons of slaves, and slaves joined his army in smaller numbers than expected.
sections.last:
At Guayaquil, Bolívar annexed the city to Colombia, and the two liberators met privately on 26 and 27 July 1822. There were no witnesses or minutes, so the content of their talks can only be inferred from later actions and letters; likely topics were reinforcements and a combined army with San Martín second to Bolívar. They differed on government: Bolívar proposed a republic, San Martín a constitutional monarchy. While San Martín was away, the minister Bernardo Monteagudo was removed by a rebellion in Lima. San Martín resigned as Protector a few days later and returned to Valparaíso. Historians give several reasons: the compromised discipline of the Army of the Andes, the rivalry between Peru and Colombia, the lack of support from Buenos Aires, O'Higgins and Cochrane, and his refusal to rule as a dictator.

His wife died in 1823 and he took their daughter Mercedes Tomasa to Europe, settling in Brussels and later in Paris. In 1837 he offered his services to Juan Manuel de Rosas against the French blockade of the Río de la Plata; Rosas declined because of San Martín's age. He bequeathed his curved saber to Rosas. After the French revolution of 1848 he moved to Boulogne-sur-Mer, almost blind and in poor health. He died there at three o'clock on 17 August 1850, shortly after news of the Argentine victory against the Anglo-French blockade.
sections.legacy:
San Martín asked in his will to be taken to the cemetery without any funeral and to be moved to Buenos Aires afterwards. He lay in the crypt of the Basilica of Notre-Dame de Boulogne from 1850 to 1861, and the unrest after Rosas's fall delayed the transfer. His remains were repatriated on 29 May 1880, under President Nicolás Avellaneda, and his mausoleum stands in the Buenos Aires Metropolitan Cathedral, in a wing expanded because he was suspected of being a freemason.

The Federals acclaimed him as a national hero of Argentina in his lifetime and after his death, while the unitarians resented his refusal to aid the Supreme Directors and his support for Rosas. The unitarian Bartolomé Mitre wrote a biography that made San Martín universally acclaimed as the Liberator of Argentina, but it introduced inaccuracies that served Mitre's political project and that later historians corrected. San Martín is regarded as a national hero of Argentina, Chile and Peru, and the Order of the Liberator General San Martín is the highest decoration the Argentine government confers. Statues stand in most Argentine cities and in Santiago and Lima, and an equestrian statue was inaugurated in Boulogne-sur-Mer on 24 October 1909.

summary: José de San Martín (1778–1850), an officer of the Spanish army born in the Guaraní missions, organised the Army of the Andes, won at Chacabuco and Maipú and sailed to Peru, whose independence he declared in 1821. After meeting Bolívar at Guayaquil he resigned and lived in Europe until his death.
references: Norberto Galasso, Seamos libres y lo demás no importa nada (Colihue, 2000)
Adolfo Espíndola, San Martín en el Ejército Español en la península (Comisión Nacional Ejecutiva del 150 Aniversario de la Revolución de Mayo, 1962)
Robert Harvey, Liberators: Latin America's Struggle For Independence (The Overlook Press, 2000)
notes: Birth year disputed (1777 or 1778; the lede gives 25 February 1778): start 1778 with circa true.

The Peninsular War paragraph is garbled: it says Solano was killed by a popular uprising but names 'Rosas' as the victim and 'suspected of being an afrancesado'; left out. Also left out: Arjonilla, Albuera, the lodge details at Alvear's house, and an unclear line that Mourgeón's guerrilla force absorbed his unit.

Chacabuco's year (1817) is inferred: the article dates the Chilean declaration of 18 February 1818 'one year after the battle of Chacabuco'; Maipú's year 1818 is from the lede. The Crossing of the Andes has no year in the article apart from 'the summer'; left undated.
Order of events: the article puts the Army of the North command (1814) before the Cuyo plan; the lede's 'time commanding the Army of the North during 1814' is followed.

The Peru section says the Army of the Andes had 4,000 men and Cochrane's navy 1,600; the fleet is also described as 'eight warships, eleven gunboats ... 12 frigates and a brig'. Counts left out as inconsistent.
San Martín's resignation in 1822: the article gives several reasons as the historians' explanations; reported as such. The Guayaquil conference's content is stated as unknown in the article.
The Protector section says the royalist leader De la Serna left Lima 'for unknown reasons' and that no documentation explains the episode at El Callao; left out.

Statue lists in Washington, New York, Beverly Hills and Manila left out for space. Remains: the article says 'between 1850 and 1861' in the cathedral crypt and also that Balcarce had a tomb made in the cemetery; the crypt years used, the tomb left out.
Rosas, whom San Martín admired, is described in the article only through San Martín's letters; no verdict on his government is given here.
